title: Steiner Forest approximation below factor two
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every feasible Steiner Forest instance \(I=(G,c,D)\), returns an edge set \(F\subseteq E(G)\) satisfying every demand and \[c(F)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\] Here \(G\) is a finite undirected graph, every edge cost is a nonnegative binary rational number, \(D\) is a finite list of vertex pairs, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum total cost of an edge set connecting each listed pair. The same \(\varepsilon\) and polynomial time bound must apply to all instances.
why: Steiner Forest models building a minimum-cost network that connects several required pairs while allowing their connections to share infrastructure. Improving its long-standing factor-two guarantee was a major unresolved threshold in approximation algorithms. The question is historically important and now has a published positive answer.
status_note: Resolved positively by the FOCS 2025 below-two approximation of Ahmadi and coauthors, with a stronger 1.994 approximation in Gupta–Traub, STOC 2026. The reviewed theorem and algorithm apply to the general Steiner Forest model. The original question and full review remain in the inactive archive; no claim of a completed Lean formalization is made.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-15; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

importance.reason: The factor-two barrier for general Steiner Forest was a central long-standing question in network-design approximation, explicitly highlighted in a standard monograph. Its resolution changes the approximation frontier for a basic multi-pair connectivity problem and has wider significance for understanding network-design guarantees.

sentences: Steiner Forest asks for a minimum-cost graph edge set connecting every specified terminal pair.
The historical question asks whether one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm achieves a fixed approximation ratio below two.
Costs may be nonnegative binary rationals, and different demands may share the chosen network.
A FOCS 2025 breakthrough answered the question, and Gupta and Traub improved the ratio to 1.994 in a paper published at STOC 2026.
This full record is therefore preserved in the archive of resolved questions.

definitions: An input lists the vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the unordered edges \(E\subseteq\binom{V}{2}\), the cost \(c_e=a_e/b_e\) of each edge with binary integers \(a_e\ge0,b_e\ge1\), and demand pairs \((s_j,t_j)\in V^2\). All lists and integers have fixed self-delimiting binary encodings, and \(N\) denotes the entire encoded bit length. A feasible solution \(F\subseteq E\) has a path from \(s_j\) to \(t_j\) in \((V,F)\) for every demand \(j\). Repeated demands and pairs with equal endpoints are allowed, and a path of length zero satisfies the latter. Different demand pairs may share edges or vertices or lie in different connected components; there is no requirement that all terminals lie in one component. All graph vertices are available for use. The cost is \(c(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c_e\), counting each chosen edge once. With nonnegative costs, a minimum exists whenever the input is feasible; a forest can attain it. Empty demand lists have optimum zero. The approximation guarantee includes every instance with zero optimum and then requires a zero-cost output. The algorithm must correctly report infeasibility if a demand cannot be connected in \(G\). It is a fixed finite deterministic Turing program, with at most \(C(N+1)^d\) bit steps for constants \(C,d\) independent of the instance. Reading rational encodings, exact arithmetic, initialization and writing the selected edges are charged. No random bits, advice or oracle is available. The question asks for some absolute saving below two, not a saving that tends to zero with input size.
answer_criterion: The historical benchmark requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence assertion or its negation. A positive answer must give a single algorithm, a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and proofs of feasibility, polynomial bit complexity and the multiplicative bound on every instance, including zero-cost optima. A conditional impossibility implication is not an unconditional negative answer. An algorithm for one connected terminal set, a restricted graph class, or a ratio approaching two from above does not establish the target for general Steiner Forest. The published below-two approximation resolves this mathematical existence question; its archival classification is not a claim that a Lean-checked proof has already been supplied.

context_blocks.text: Williamson and Shmoys call this the generalized Steiner tree problem in their 2011 list of open problems. Their Problem 6 asks for an improvement on the factor-two guarantee for the multi-pair connectivity problem. The original threshold question is retained here; it is not replaced by the harder task of determining the best possible approximation constant.

Ahmadi, Gholami, Hajiaghayi, Jabbarzade and Mahdavi broke the barrier in their FOCS 2025 paper, giving a fixed improvement of order \(10^{-11}\) below two. This already answers the historical existence question.

Gupta and Traub subsequently prove a \(1.994\)-approximation for general Steiner Forest. Their preprint was posted on 23 November 2025 and the paper appeared at STOC 2026. Its Theorem 1.1 and polynomial-time algorithm, analyzed in Section 7, give a further published positive resolution.

The reviewed results use the same general undirected multi-pair problem as the card. Better ratios for ordinary Steiner Tree concern a special case; unresolved questions about a particular linear-programming relaxation do not reopen the existence of a below-two approximation for Steiner Forest.
